cases.answerText: **Yes.** Under the 2022 NYC Building Code, glazing in a fixed or operable panel of a swinging door is considered a hazardous location and therefore requires safety glazing, unless an exception applies (BC §§ 2406.4, 2406.4.1). Exceptions are a glazed opening too small for a 3-inch-diameter sphere to pass through, decorative glazing, curved glazing used in a revolving door, and glazing in a commercial refrigerated-cabinet door.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and exception scope match frozen source; no unsupported addition identified in displayed answer.
cases.answerText: Yes. BC 2406.4.1 expressly lists “Decorative glazing” as an exception to treating glazing in fixed or operable panels of swinging, sliding, and bifold doors as a hazardous location (BC § 2406.4.1).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and exception scope match frozen source; no unsupported addition identified in displayed answer.
cases.answerText: **Yes.** Under 2022 NYC BC § 2406.4.2, glazing in an individual fixed or operable panel is hazardous when its nearest vertical edge is within a 24-inch arc of either vertical edge of the closed door and its bottom exposed edge is less than 60 inches above the walking surface. The stated 24-inch and 40-inch measurements meet those conditions; with no exception, the glazing is a hazardous location.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and exception scope match frozen source; no unsupported addition identified in displayed answer.
cases.answerText: Yes. BC 2406.4.2 expressly excepts glazing where “there is an intervening wall or other permanent barrier between the door and glazing.” If that condition applies, the glazing is not treated as a hazardous location under this door-adjacent rule. (BC § 2406.4.2)

cases.answerText: No. BC 2406.4.3’s first condition requires the exposed area of an individual pane to be **greater than 9 square feet**. An 8-square-foot pane does not meet that area trigger, so it does not satisfy the specific four-condition test, which requires all four conditions. The listed exceptions do not change this area comparison. (BC § 2406.4.3)

cases.label: correct_useful

cases.answerText: Yes. BC 2406.4.5 expressly says the hazardous-location rule applies to “single glazing and all panes in multiple glazing” when the stated glazing and height conditions are met. Its exception is limited to glazing more than 60 inches, measured horizontally and in a straight line, from the water’s edge of a bathtub, hot tub, spa, whirlpool, or swimming pool; it does not list showers. (BC § 2406.4.5)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, dimensions and applicable exceptions match frozen source text.
cases.answerText: Yes. BC 2406.4.5 expressly excepts glazing “more than 60 inches (1524 mm), measured horizontally and in a straight line,” from the water’s edge of a bathtub (as well as the other listed water features). Thus, bathtub-facing glazing at the stated distance falls within that exception. (BC § 2406.4.5)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, dimensions and applicable exceptions match frozen source text.
cases.answerText: **Yes, provided the stated dimensions are measured as BC 2406.4.7 specifies and its exception does not apply.** The section treats glazing as hazardous when it is less than 60 inches above the bottom landing and within a 60-inch horizontal arc that is less than 180 degrees from the bottom tread nosing. At 40 inches, the height condition is met. But glazing protected by a guard complying with BC §§ 1015 and 1607.8 is excepted if the glass plane is more than 18 inches from the guard. (BC § 2406.4.7)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, dimensions and applicable exceptions match frozen source text.
cases.answerText: No. Under 2022 NYC BC 2406.4.7, the exception applies only when the glass plane is **greater than 18 inches** from a guard complying with Sections 1015 and 1607.8; exactly 18 inches does not meet that exception. (BC § 2406.4.7)

cases.answerText: **4 inches (101.6 mm) minimum.** For a toilet room outside a dwelling unit, BC 1210.2.1 requires a smooth, hard, nonabsorbent vertical base at the floor-wall intersection extending upward onto the walls at least that height. The stated 6-inch minimum applies only to Group I-1, R-1, and R-2 occupancies; an office is not among those listed exceptions. (BC § 1210.2.1)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, dimensions and applicable exceptions match frozen source text.
cases.answerText: Yes. BC 1210.2.1 requires a vertical base extending at least 6 inches up the walls for Group R-2, as an express exception to the general 4-inch minimum for the covered toilet, bathing, and shower room floors outside dwelling units (BC § 1210.2.1).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Dimensional threshold, calculation or exception matches frozen source key; no material false addition identified.
cases.answerText: At least **4 feet (1,220 mm) above the floor**. In a public toilet room, walls and partitions within 2 feet (609.6 mm) of a water closet must have a smooth, hard, nonabsorbent surface to that height; the stated exception for a toilet room that is not accessible to the public does not apply to your scenario (BC § 1210.2.2).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Dimensional threshold, calculation or exception matches frozen source key; no material false addition identified.
cases.answerText: Yes. BC 1210.2.2 expressly excepts a toilet room “that [is] not accessible to the public” and has “not more than one water closet” from its wall-and-partition surface and moisture-resistance requirements. So a nonpublic toilet room with exactly one WC qualifies for this exception to those requirements; the exception does not, by itself, waive other code requirements. (BC § 1210.2.2)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Dimensional threshold, calculation or exception matches frozen source key; no material false addition identified.
cases.answerText: For a 200 sf room, 10 percent is **20 sf of minimum net glazed area**. BC 1205.2.1 also requires every opening providing required natural light to have at least **12 sf of glazed area**; 20 sf exceeds that minimum. For Group R-3, the rule is the greater of 10 percent or 12 sf, which is also 20 sf here (BC § 1205.2.1).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Dimensional threshold, calculation or exception matches frozen source key; no material false addition identified.
cases.answerText: No. For Group R-3, the required net glazed area is the greater of 10% of the room’s floor area or 12 square feet. For a 100-sf room, that is 12 sf, so 10 sf is insufficient under BC § 1205.2.1.

cases.label: correct_useful

cases.answerText: The ordinary minimum is **8 feet (2438.4 mm) in any plan dimension** for a habitable space other than a kitchen (2022 NYC BC § 1208.1). That is the baseline before applying any exception; your question excludes exceptions.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Dimensional threshold, calculation or exception matches frozen source key; no material false addition identified.
cases.answerText: Under the 2022 NYC Building Code, kitchens and kitchenettes must have at least **3 feet (914.4 mm) of clear passageway** between counter fronts and appliances (BC § 1208.1).

cases.answerText: **No.** Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, the shower compartment must meet both a minimum **900-square-inch interior cross-sectional area** and a minimum **30-inch least dimension**. A 950-square-inch area meets the area minimum, but 28 inches is below the separate dimension minimum; the area does not authorize that shorter dimension (PC § 417.4). The section’s measurement method is stated to apply “Except as required in Section 404”; the supplied evidence does not include Section 404, so any Section 404-specific measurement requirement cannot be resolved here.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Rule, calculation, table entry or exception matches frozen source key; hub-drain answer correctly distinguishes pipe form.
cases.answerText: PC 417.4 requires the shower compartment’s minimum required area and dimension to continue to **at least 70 inches (1,778 mm) above the shower drain outlet**. The measurement is taken at the finished interior dimension, beginning at the top of the threshold and at a point tangent to its centerline, **except as required in PC 404**. The supplied evidence does not include PC 404, so whether that exception changes the rule for a particular case cannot be determined here.

cases.answerText: Yes. Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, tempered water must be delivered from lavatories and group wash fixtures located in public toilet facilities provided for customers, patrons, and visitors. It must be delivered through an approved temperature-limiting device conforming to ASSE 1070; where point-of-use heaters are installed, the outlet temperature must instead be regulated to provide tempered water (PC § 416.5).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Rule, calculation, table entry or exception matches frozen source key; hub-drain answer correctly distinguishes pipe form.
cases.answerText: Yes. In the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, PC 416.5 expressly provides an exception: “Where point of use heaters are installed, outlet water temperature shall be regulated to provide tempered water.” Thus, a point-of-use heater outlet regulated to provide tempered water meets the condition stated in that exception. (PC § 416.5)

cases.answerText: **No.** Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, urinals may replace no more than 50% of the required water closets in each bathroom or toilet room, so replacing 60% exceeds the limit (PC § 419.2).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Rule, calculation, table entry or exception matches frozen source key; hub-drain answer correctly distinguishes pipe form.
cases.answerText: **Four** may be replaced under PC 419.2’s percentage limit alone: 50% of 8 required water closets is 4. This answers only the stated percentage limit, not any other applicable requirement. (PC § 419.2)

cases.note: Rule, calculation, table entry or exception matches frozen source key; hub-drain answer correctly distinguishes pipe form.
cases.answerText: A floor drain must have a drain outlet at least **3 inches (76 mm) in diameter** under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code (PC § 412.3).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Rule, calculation, table entry or exception matches frozen source key; hub-drain answer correctly distinguishes pipe form.
cases.answerText: **No.** Under 2022 NYC PC 412.3, a floor-drain outlet must be at least **3 inches (76 mm) in diameter**. A 2-inch outlet is 1 inch below that minimum and does not meet the ordinary requirement. (PC § 412.3)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Rule, calculation, table entry or exception matches frozen source key; hub-drain answer correctly distinguishes pipe form.
cases.answerText: **Yes.** Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, rooms containing automatic clothes washers in the central washing facilities of multiple-family dwellings must have floor drains positioned to readily drain the entire floor area. The drains must have outlets at least 3 inches in diameter and lint strainers (PC § 412.4).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Rule, calculation, table entry or exception matches frozen source key; hub-drain answer correctly distinguishes pipe form.
cases.answerText: **No.** For the rooms covered by 2022 PC 412.4, a 3-inch outlet meets the stated minimum diameter, but the drain must also be provided with a lint strainer. The separate floor-drain rule requires removable strainers and contains no exception that waives PC 412.4’s lint-strainer requirement. (PC §§ 412.4, 412.2)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Rule, calculation, table entry or exception matches frozen source key; hub-drain answer correctly distinguishes pipe form.
cases.answerText: No. Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, drainage piping may not decrease in size in the direction of flow. A downstream reduction from 4 inches to 3 inches is prohibited unless it is the expressly stated exception: a 4-inch-by-3-inch water-closet connection is not considered a reduction in size (PC § 704.2).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Rule, calculation, table entry or exception matches frozen source key; hub-drain answer correctly distinguishes pipe form.
cases.answerText: No. Under 2022 NYC PC § 704.2, a 4-inch by 3-inch water-closet connection “shall not be considered as a reduction in size,” so it is not treated as a prohibited reduction under that section.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Rule, calculation, table entry or exception matches frozen source key; hub-drain answer correctly distinguishes pipe form.
cases.answerText: No. The 2022 NYC Plumbing Code’s Table 706.3 shows a dash for a sanitary tee under “horizontal to horizontal,” so it is not permitted for that change in direction under the table. PC § 706.3 requires changes in direction to use fittings in accordance with the table. The table’s note (c) addresses a limitation on double sanitary tees; it does not change the dash for horizontal-to-horizontal.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Rule, calculation, table entry or exception matches frozen source key; hub-drain answer correctly distinguishes pipe form.
cases.answerText: Yes. PC Table 706.3 marks a long sweep as permitted for all three patterns: horizontal-to-vertical, vertical-to-horizontal, and horizontal-to-horizontal. The table’s footnotes restrict certain other fitting types, but none is attached to the long-sweep row (PC § 706.3).

cases.note: Numeric1inch matches source, but answer restricts it to pipe form; same attachment ambiguity as paired flush-hub question. Exclude both from adjusted score pending professional adjudication.
cases.answerText: The **pipe form** of a hub drain must extend at least **1 inch (25 mm)** above the water-impervious floor. PC 802.3.2 also permits the drain to be in the form of a hub. (PC § 802.3.2)

cases.label: ungradable_source_or_key_ambiguity
cases.note: Wording permits two readings of whether elevation modifies hub and pipe or pipe alone. Frozen no-key and conditional answer require professional adjudication. Do not count as an established model error or success.
cases.answerText: **Flushness alone does not determine the answer.** Under 2022 NYC Plumbing Code § 802.3.2, a hub drain must be either “in the form of a hub” or a pipe extending at least 1 inch (25 mm) above the water-impervious floor. A flush drain satisfies the section only if it is in the form of a hub; a flush pipe does not.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, numeric threshold and exception match frozen source text.
cases.answerText: Generally, no: PC 1002.1 states, “A fixture shall not be double trapped.” But Exception 1 says the section does not apply to fixtures with integral traps; it does not affirmatively permit double trapping for them. (PC § 1002.1)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, numeric threshold and exception match frozen source text.
cases.answerText: **30 inches (762 mm) maximum.** For an ordinary fixture with no applicable exception, measure horizontally from the **centerline of the fixture outlet** to the **centerline of the trap inlet** (2022 NYC PC § 1002.1).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, numeric threshold and exception match frozen source text.
cases.answerText: If the occupancy is not Group R-3, an intake on an 18-foot-wide lot must be at the centerline between the lot lines—9 feet from each line. Group R-3 occupancies are expressly exempt from MC 401.4, so the special rule does not apply to them. (MC § 401.4)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, numeric threshold and exception match frozen source text.
cases.answerText: Yes. The supplied 2022 NYC Mechanical Code text expressly states: “Exception: Group R-3 occupancies are not required to comply with Section 401.4.” (MC § 401.4)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, numeric threshold and exception match frozen source text.
cases.answerText: No. For an intake opening in a residential occupancy, Table 401.5 requires screen openings to be at least 1/4 inch and no more than 1/2 inch, measured in any direction. A 3/4-inch opening exceeds the maximum. (MC § 401.5)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, numeric threshold and exception match frozen source text.
cases.answerText: No. For intake openings in other-than-residential occupancies, Table 401.5 requires an opening size **greater than 1/4 inch** and no greater than 1 inch, measured in any direction. Exactly 1/4 inch does not meet the lower limit (MC § 401.5).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Source-key match, including transfer-air limits and correct CO/NO2 units and OR condition.
cases.answerText: **No.** Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, the outdoor air required under Section 403.3.1.1 may not be recirculated. Air supplied in excess of that required quantity may be recirculated, subject to the stated restrictions—for example, between dwelling units or dissimilar occupancies, and in certain spaces requiring mechanical exhaust (MC § 403.2.1). A separate exception allows the minimum required outdoor-air rate to be reduced when a registered design professional demonstrates an engineered ventilation system designed under ASHRAE 62.1’s Indoor Air Quality Procedure; that is a permitted reduction, not substitution of recirculated air for required outdoor air (MC § 403.2).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Source-key match, including transfer-air limits and correct CO/NO2 units and OR condition.
cases.answerText: No. Under 2022 NYC MC § 403.2.1, ventilation air may not be recirculated from one dwelling unit to another. Although the section generally allows recirculation of air in excess of required outdoor air as part of supply air, it expressly excludes this dwelling-unit-to-dwelling-unit transfer.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Source-key match, including transfer-air limits and correct CO/NO2 units and OR condition.
cases.answerText: **Yes, in principle.** MC 403.2.2 permits air transferred from occupiable spaces to serve as makeup air for required exhaust in baths and similar spaces, except where recirculation from such spaces is prohibited by Table 403.3.1.1. The transfer and exhaust airflow must be sufficient to meet the table rates, and required outdoor airflow must be introduced directly into such spaces, into the occupied spaces from which air is transferred, or both (MC §§ 403.2.2, 403.3.1.1).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Source-key match, including transfer-air limits and correct CO/NO2 units and OR condition.
cases.answerText: No. Transferred air may serve as makeup air for required exhaust, subject to the stated recirculation exception, but it does not let you omit required outdoor air. MC 403.2.2 requires the applicable transfer-air and exhaust flow rates to be met, and requires the outdoor airflow to be introduced directly into the exhaust-served space, into the occupied space from which air is transferred, or into both. (MC § 403.2.2; § 403.3.1.1) Separately, MC 403.2 provides that the minimum outdoor-air rate may be reduced where a registered design professional demonstrates that an engineered ventilation system is designed in accordance with the ASHRAE 62.1 Indoor Air Quality Procedure. (MC § 403.2)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Source-key match, including transfer-air limits and correct CO/NO2 units and OR condition.
cases.answerText: Both **carbon monoxide detectors and nitrogen dioxide detectors** control intermittent operation of enclosed-garage ventilation; the system must operate automatically when it detects **25 ppm CO or 500 ppb NO₂**. Install the detectors according to their manufacturers’ instructions (2022 NYC MC § 404.1).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Source-key match, including transfer-air limits and correct CO/NO2 units and OR condition.
cases.answerText: For intermittent mechanical ventilation systems serving enclosed parking garages, the system must operate automatically when either carbon monoxide reaches **25 ppm** or nitrogen dioxide reaches **500 ppb** (2022 NYC MC § 404.1). Detectors must be installed in accordance with the manufacturers’ instructions.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Source-key match, including transfer-air limits and correct CO/NO2 units and OR condition.
cases.answerText: Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, automatic operation may reduce enclosed parking garage ventilation to **no less than 0.05 cfm per square foot of floor area**. The system must also be capable of producing **0.75 cfm per square foot** (MC § 404.2).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion and conditions match source key.
cases.answerText: The system must be capable of producing **0.75 cfm per square foot of floor area** (0.0038 m³/s per m²). This is the required ventilation airflow capacity under 2022 NYC MC § 404.2.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion and conditions match source key.
cases.answerText: Yes. Under 2022 NYC MC 504.6, an installation exhausting more than 200 cfm must be provided with makeup air; 250 cfm exceeds that threshold (MC § 504.6).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion and conditions match source key.
cases.answerText: No. Under 2022 NYC MC § 504.6, the enclosure-opening method requires an opening of at least 100 square inches, so 90 square inches is 10 square inches short. The stated alternative is makeup air provided by other approved means.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion and conditions match source key.
cases.answerText: Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, ducts and air-transfer openings permitted through fire walls must generally have **listed fire dampers and smoke dampers**, installed according to their listings (MC § 607.5.1). The exception removes the smoke-damper requirement—not the fire-damper requirement—when air continues to move and the air-handling system prevents exhaust or return-air recirculation during fire emergencies or loss of normal power, using standby power in accordance with NYC Building Code Chapter 27.

cases.label: incorrect_minor
cases.note: Correctly retains fire damper, but paraphrases standby protection as an alternative to fire-emergency protection. Source requires the continuing-air/no-recirculation arrangement under the stated emergency and power-loss circumstances. Imprecise exception explanation; core no remains correct.
cases.answerText: **No.** MC 607.5.1 requires both listed fire and smoke dampers for the described firewall penetrations. Its exception waives only the smoke damper when the air continues to move and the system prevents exhaust or return-air recirculation under fire-emergency conditions, or standby power provides that protection during loss of normal power. It does not waive the fire damper. (MC § 607.5.1)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion and conditions match source key.
cases.answerText: **No.** MC 607.5.2 says ducts and air-transfer openings may not penetrate interior exit stairway enclosures except as permitted by BC §§ 1023.5 and 1024.6, as applicable. Its fire-damper requirement for penetrations of fire barriers does not itself grant permission to penetrate a stair enclosure; the cited Building Code provisions govern whether that penetration is permitted. Those two provisions are not included in the supplied evidence, so whether a particular penetration is allowed under them cannot be determined here. (MC § 607.5.2)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core conclusion and conditions match source key.
cases.answerText: No. The 2022 NYC MC § 607.5.2 exception expressly requires the fire barrier to be in an area “other than Group H,” so this one-hour, sprinklered ducted-HVAC exception does not include Group H areas. It also requires a rating of 1 hour or less, sprinklers throughout the building under the specified Building Code provisions, and a qualifying continuous sheet-metal HVAC duct system.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Correctly distinguishes303.3 exception1 from narrower303.3.1 sleeping-room installation provision; matches pre-output official-source addendum.
cases.answerText: **No—not under FGC 303.3’s direct-vent exception**, which expressly applies only in rooms “other than those used for sleeping purposes.” But a separate, narrower provision deems a gas-fired direct-vent space-heating appliance used to provide heat in a sleeping room to be outside that room, provided the appliance and installation comply with FGC 303.3.1.1 through 303.3.1.7 (FGC §§ 303.3, 303.3.1). That is not a blanket allowance for any direct-vent gas appliance. The supplied evidence does not include all seven referenced conditions, so whether a particular installation qualifies cannot be determined from this packet.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Correct conditional bathroom exception, input threshold, infiltration method or opening dimension.
cases.answerText: **Yes—provided** the appliance is installed in accordance with both the conditions of its listing and the manufacturer’s instructions. FGC 303.3 generally prohibits appliances in bathrooms, but its direct-vent exception applies in rooms other than those used for sleeping purposes and expressly covers appliances obtaining all combustion air directly from outdoors. A bathroom is not excluded by that exception merely because it is a bathroom. (FGC § 303.3)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Correct conditional bathroom exception, input threshold, infiltration method or opening dimension.
cases.answerText: No—assuming this is a fuel-burning appliance and 400,000 Btu/h is its input rating, it cannot rely solely on indoor combustion air. FGC 304.5 requires combustion, ventilation, and dilution air to be obtained “solely from the outdoors” for fuel-burning appliances with input greater than 350,000 Btu/h; 400,000 Btu/h exceeds that threshold. (FGC § 304.5)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Correct conditional bathroom exception, input threshold, infiltration method or opening dimension.
cases.answerText: For fuel-burning appliances **not covered by the outdoor-only exception**, use FGC § 304.5.2, the known air-infiltration-rate method: 0.30 ACH is less than 0.40 ACH, which triggers that method. Use Equation 3-1 for appliances other than fan-assisted and Equation 3-2 for fan-assisted appliances. The exception requires combustion, ventilation, and dilution air to come solely from outdoors for an appliance with input greater than 350,000 Btu/h. (FGC §§ 304.5, 304.5.2)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Correct conditional bathroom exception, input threshold, infiltration method or opening dimension.
cases.answerText: The minimum dimension of an outdoor combustion-air opening is **3 inches (76.2 mm)**. The opening size must also comply with applicable New York City Department of Environmental Protection rules (FGC § 304.6).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Correct conditional bathroom exception, input threshold, infiltration method or opening dimension.
cases.answerText: **No.** Under 2022 NYC FGC § 304.6, an air opening’s minimum dimension must be at least **3 inches**; making a 2-inch-wide opening taller does not satisfy that minimum. The section separately requires the opening size to comply with any applicable New York City Department of Environmental Protection rules, which are not supplied here.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core decision, dimension, installation condition or test-isolation requirement matches frozen source text.
cases.answerText: Yes. Under the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code, fittings installed in concealed locations are limited to threaded elbows, tees and couplings, or welded fittings; threaded elbows are expressly permitted (FGC § 404.5).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core decision, dimension, installation condition or test-isolation requirement matches frozen source text.
cases.answerText: No. FGC 404.5 limits concealed-location fittings to threaded elbows, tees, couplings, and welded fittings; it does not include unions (FGC § 404.5). Separately, FGC 403.10.1.1 prohibits unions, with an exception permitting them downstream of the appliance valve under § 411.1.6. That exception requires the union to be accessible and within 6 feet of the appliance; it does not add unions to § 404.5’s concealed-location list (FGC §§ 403.10.1.1, 411.1.6).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core decision, dimension, installation condition or test-isolation requirement matches frozen source text.
cases.answerText: Under the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code, the protective sleeve must extend at least **1 inch (25.4 mm) beyond the inside** of the foundation wall and at least **4 inches (101.6 mm) beyond the outside**. The code also allows a different projection if otherwise required by the gas provider. (FGC § 404.6)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core decision, dimension, installation condition or test-isolation requirement matches frozen source text.
cases.answerText: **No.** For underground gas piping installed below grade through a building’s outer foundation or basement wall, FGC 404.6 requires the annular space between the gas pipe and sleeve to be waterproofed and sealed (FGC § 404.6). The supplied provision states no exception to that requirement.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core decision, dimension, installation condition or test-isolation requirement matches frozen source text.
cases.answerText: Outdoor gas piping crossing a roof must be at least **3½ inches (88.9 mm) above the roof surface** (FGC § 404.9).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core decision, dimension, installation condition or test-isolation requirement matches frozen source text.
cases.answerText: No. If the gas piping is installed outdoors on the roof, FGC 404.9 says it “shall not be concealed.” It must also be elevated at least 3½ inches above the roof surface and identified under FGC 401.5. (FGC §§ 404.9, 401.5)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core decision, dimension, installation condition or test-isolation requirement matches frozen source text.
cases.answerText: FGC 404.13 requires the trench to be graded so the pipe has firm, substantially continuous bearing on the trench bottom.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core decision, dimension, installation condition or test-isolation requirement matches frozen source text.
cases.answerText: **No.** Under the 2022 NYC FGC, the trench must be graded so the pipe has “a firm, substantially continuous bearing on the bottom of the trench.” Widely spaced isolated mounds alone do not provide substantially continuous bearing (FGC § 404.13).

cases.answerText: **No.** Under the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code, underground piping beneath a building is prohibited unless it is encased in a wrought-iron or steel-pipe conduit designed to withstand superimposed loads. Merely placing the pipe beneath the building without that conduit does not satisfy the stated exception (FGC § 404.14). The conduit must also meet the section’s corrosion-protection and installation requirements; the supplied evidence does not establish those details.

cases.answerText: Under the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code, appliances or equipment designed for operating pressures below the piping test pressure must be isolated by disconnecting them and capping their outlet(s). When the gas is energized, check the affected piping and joints with noncorrosive leak-detecting fluid or another approved leak-detecting method (FGC § 406.3.3).

cases.answerText: **Yes, if** the piping system is connected to appliances or equipment designed for operating pressures below the test pressure. In that case, those appliances or equipment must be isolated by disconnecting them and capping the outlet(s), and the affected piping and joints must be checked for leaks when gas is energized, using noncorrosive leak-detecting fluid or another approved leak-detecting method (FGC § 406.3.3).

cases.answerText: No. Under the supplied 2022 NYC Fire Code text, hot ashes must not be deposited in a combustible container (FC § 305.2). The exception allows a 2-foot separation from other combustible materials only when the ashes are placed in a covered, noncombustible container on a noncombustible floor, ground surface, or stand; it does not permit using a combustible container.

cases.answerText: FC 307.4 specifies a portable fire extinguisher with a **minimum 4-A rating** as one permitted option. The alternative is other approved on-site fire-extinguishing equipment, such as a garden hose connected to an approved water supply (FC § 307.4).

cases.answerText: Yes. FC 310.2(4.3) prohibits smoking in Group M occupancies, except smoking non-tobacco smoking products in a non-tobacco hookah establishment in accordance with FC 310.7. Since the question excludes an authorized hookah-establishment exception, that exception does not apply; the stated Group M occupancy is subject to the prohibition (FC § 310.2).

cases.answerText: Yes. FC 310.2(4.1) prohibits smoking in cellars and basements **except in R-3 occupancies**. The text expressly excludes R-3 from that particular prohibition; it does not, by itself, establish that smoking is permitted in every R-3 cellar or basement, since other FC 310 prohibitions may still apply. (FC § 310.2(4.1))

cases.answerText: **Maximum: 1 gallon.** FC 314.4 limits liquid fuel in a displayed vehicle’s tank to “one-eighth tank or 2.5 gallons (9.5 L) (whichever is less).” For an 8-gallon tank, one-eighth is 1 gallon, which is less than 2.5 gallons. (FC § 314.4)

cases.answerText: For the covered exterior openings, mark **“SHAFTWAY” in red letters at least 6 inches (152 mm) high on a white background**. Place the warning sign so it is readily discernible from outside. The rule applies to outside openings accessible to the department that open directly onto a hoistway or shaftway communicating between two or more floors (FC § 316.2.1).

cases.answerText: **No.** Interior door or window openings to a hoistway or shaftway must be marked “SHAFTWAY” in red letters at least 6 inches high on a white background, with the sign readily discernible. But marking is not required when the opening is readily discernible as an opening onto a shaftway by its construction or arrangement (FC § 316.2.2).

cases.answerText: FC 505.1 requires address numbers to be at least **4 inches (102 mm) high**, with a minimum **½-inch (12.7 mm) stroke width**. They must contrast with their background and be plainly discernible from the public street or frontage space. FC 505.1 also requires compliance with the Building Code, the NYC Housing Maintenance Code, and the borough president’s requirements. The supplied Building Code provision specifies characters at least 4 inches high and 0.5 inch wide, except as otherwise provided by the applicable borough president’s rules (BC § 501.2); the Housing Maintenance Code text and borough-president rules are not supplied.

cases.answerText: No. Under the supplied 2022 NYC Fire Code FC 505.1 text, address numbers must contrast with their background; being larger than the four-inch minimum does not replace that separate contrast requirement (FC § 505.1). The identification must also be plainly discernible from the public street or frontage space.

When access is restricted by locked doors or other building openings, or immediate access **“would be needed”** for lifesaving or firefighting purposes in a fire or other emergency, the department may require a key box in an approved location; those conditions do not make the requirement automatic without a department requirement. (FC § 506.2.2)

cases.answerText: No. ZR 43-22 says a yard or rear yard equivalent in a Manufacturing District may not be higher than curb level, but expressly states that compliance does not require disturbing natural grade. It separately prohibits structures above ground level in a required yard or rear yard equivalent except as allowed by ZR 43-23. (ZR § 43-22; § 43-23.)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, dimensional threshold and cited scope match frozen source key.
cases.answerText: Yes. In Manufacturing Districts, ZR 43-22 first states that a yard or rear yard equivalent “shall not be higher than curb level,” then provides that the section does not require disturbing natural grade to comply. Thus curb level is the ordinary upper limit, subject to that natural-grade proviso. (ZR § 43-22)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, dimensional threshold and cited scope match frozen source key.
cases.answerText: **23 feet above curb level** is the maximum height for energy infrastructure equipment and accessory mechanical equipment permitted in a required yard or rear yard equivalent in any Manufacturing District (ZR § 43-23(a)(3)). This limit is stated for all such equipment; the separate rear-yard building and solar-canopy height limits address different obstructions. ZR § 43-23 also refers to ZR §§ 23-311 and 23-341, but the supplied text of § 43-23 itself states the 23-foot limit for this equipment.

cases.answerText: **No.** If ZR 43-23 applies to the site, its listed wall obstruction permission covers walls no higher than eight feet that are not roofed or part of a building; a freestanding nine-foot wall exceeds that limit. The section applies in Manufacturing Districts. (ZR § 43-23.) This answers only whether the wall qualifies under that listed permission; the supplied text is insufficient to determine whether a separate obstruction provision could authorize it.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, dimensional threshold and cited scope match frozen source key.
cases.answerText: Under ZR 43-24, in all Manufacturing Districts, the width or depth of a yard or rear yard equivalent is measured **perpendicular to lot lines**. The supplied text does not specify a particular lot-line segment or add a separate measurement method.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion, dimensional threshold and cited scope match frozen source key.
cases.answerText: **No.** In Manufacturing Districts, ZR 43-24 requires a yard’s width or depth to be measured perpendicular to lot lines, so a longer diagonal distance cannot substitute for that measurement (ZR § 43-24). This answer is limited to the rule’s stated scope.
